purpose: Registration fragment for the Airlock Plan application: the app's own MCP binding only. The app declares its own service; the UserIO account belongs to the Universal UserIO app and is reached through that app's operations, not through a binding on its resource. Merges into integrations/airlock-apps/apps.json.

_canon.question: How does an application reach the MCP resource of another application?
_canon.answer: Option (a): the application declares a need (a manifest binding) for that resource and the platform binds it. The credential never leaves the platform: the broker injects it per call and scrubs it from the response. Option (b) is the authorization half of the same mechanism (resource_grants 'use' lets a principal other than the owner bind the resource), not an alternative to declaring the need. Option (c) is not a platform mechanism: service_read exists only in the app template (integrations/airlock-apps/main.go:96), the core exposes no cross-application call route, and the agent-scoped call injects only the credential, not the caller (service/runtime/integrations.go:113-146).
evidence: db/queries/resource_needs.sql:117-119 - 'a need's slug resolves to its bound resource row. The credential proxy then keys off the resolved resource's own id/owner, never the calling agent - that is what lets one resource back many agents.'
service/needs/bind.go:509-600 (bindExisting) - the binder must hold authz.ResourceUse on the resource (owner or a 'use' grant); the credential lives in agent_mcp_servers, not in the app.
db/migrations/012_platform_runtime.sql:59-75 - no uniqueness on mcp_server_id, so one resource may back the needs of many agents.
live: resource 365c1a4b (Universal UserIO) backs the needs userio_owner of universal-userio and userio_owner of airlockplan - the platform already runs that way.
_canon.app_level_rule: The shared adapter's slot selection (integrations/airlock-apps/main.go:59-69) picks one binding per calling principal, so the bindings of one application are slots of ONE service. Two bindings of one principal are ambiguous (the first match wins) and the plan's second binding put the owner's personal UserIO credential behind a shared slot that every administrator of the app could reach. The application therefore declares its own service only, and the platform's contract test says so: integrations/airlock-apps/plan_binding_test.go.
_canon.personal_resource_rule: docs/AIRLOCK_FIVE_APPS_TASK.md:188-190,210 - the callback picks the slot strictly by principal and the owner's token is never substituted into Oleg's slot. The live feed stays the owner's: the app's own MCP refuses it on the platform-facing endpoint (reason 'scope') and the product refuses it to any other administrator of the platform.

principal.note: No principal: the service of the app is shared, so every administrator of the app reaches the app's own MCP. A principal would make the slot personal and would exclude the second administrator from the board.

platform_rule.text: binding.user_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM CASE WHEN need.binding_mode='shared' THEN NULL ELSE $1::uuid END AND (m.owner_principal_id = creator.id OR EXISTS (resource_grants with 'use' for creator))
platform_rule.consequence: A shared MCP resource resolves only while its owner_principal_id equals the binding creator (binding.created_by_user_id), or the creator holds a 'use' grant.
platform_rule.verified_by: read-only SELECT: the plan's binding (dad13179-9eb7-4554-8157-3db7d2dffe39) points at resource 200e258f (owner 5e438326), created_by_user_id=5e438326 -> the rule holds.

defects_found_and_fixed.symptom: the curated wrapper service_read routed every airlock_* operation to the UserIO MCP for the owner, and the second administrator matched no slot at all
defects_found_and_fixed.cause: the adapter picks one binding per calling principal (first exact match, then a single-binding fallback). Two bindings of the same principal are ambiguous, and the plan's own service was not distinguishable from a foreign resource in the same manifest.
defects_found_and_fixed.fix: the plan declares one binding - its own service, without a principal - so every caller of the app reaches the app's own MCP. The contract test states the rule for the whole registry: every binding of an app points at that app's own product host, and no principal has two slots.

defects_found_and_fixed.symptom: the owner's personal UserIO credential was reachable through the app for every administrator of the app
defects_found_and_fixed.cause: a shared binding on the owner's personal UserIO resource: the platform injects the resource credential for any caller of the app, so the second administrator (an admin member of the app) received the owner's private chats.
defects_found_and_fixed.fix: the plan holds no binding on the UserIO resource any more. notes: The app container is idle-reaped by the platform ('stopping idle container' in the backend log). It is reconciled again on the next admitted request or with POST /api/v1/agents/{id}/start; the agent token lives in the container environment, so a probe that needs the token must start the container first.
The app's own operation allowlist (apps.json operations) still lists only the airlock_* operations; the userio.* tools of the Universal UserIO app are exposed by that app, not by the plan.

The live tools are served by the app's own MCP but only on the scoped (narrow token) endpoint of the product: the live feed reads a personal account, and the platform does not substitute the owner's token for somebody else's call.
